title: The Subsidy Cliff: Washington Let Your Health Insurance Discount Expire, Then Sent You the Bill
dek: Both parties saw the end date on Obamacare's bigger tax credits coming for years. Premiums jumped, 2.6 million people dropped coverage, and 2027's price tags land two days before the midterms.
body:
## Previously, on your health insurance

Open enrollment for 2027 health coverage starts November 1 [11][12]. That's two days before the midterms, which makes it the political version of mailing someone their credit card statement on the morning of a job interview.

Here's what we're talking about. Over 20 million Americans buy their own health insurance on the Affordable Care Act marketplaces [11]. In 2021, Congress passed the American Rescue Plan, which made the tax credits that help pay those premiums more generous and lifted the cap that cut people off at 400 percent of the poverty line [7]. In 2022 the Inflation Reduction Act extended the bigger credits, but only through the end of 2025 [7]. Then the end of 2025 arrived, as dates tend to do, and the bigger credits expired [11].

So this is the story of a discount with an expiration date that everybody in Washington could read, and of how they spent the year before it ran out yelling about who would get blamed instead of reading it.

## Two parties, one cliff

Let's start with the people who wrote the expiration date. Democrats built the enhanced credits as a temporary program, renewed them as a temporary program, and set the end date for December 31, 2025 [7]. That's a little like building a bridge that stops halfway across the river and then campaigning on how much you love the far shore.

Then came the fall of 2025, when health insurance affordability was a central fight in a 43-day government shutdown, the longest in U.S. history [7]. The deal that reopened the government promised the Senate a vote on keeping the credits [7]. The vote was held on December 11. The Democratic bill, a three-year extension, got 51 votes to 48, with four Republicans on board: Susan Collins, Josh Hawley, Lisa Murkowski and Dan Sullivan [5]. In the Senate, 51 votes is a majority, and also, thanks to the filibuster, a loss; it needed 60 [5]. The Republican alternative, which skipped the extension and offered health savings account deposits of $1,000 to $1,500 to some enrollees, also got 51 to 48, and also lost [5]. The Senate held two votes, got the same score both times, and called it a day. That's not legislating. That's a coin landing on its edge twice and everyone going home.

The president's contribution, during the shutdown, was a post recommending the money "BE SENT DIRECTLY TO THE PEOPLE" so they could buy "MUCH BETTER, HEALTHCARE" [8]. Axios noted the post came with no detailed policy proposal attached [8]. Which is fine. Nobody has ever been denied a claim by a proposal that doesn't exist.

## The House does something, which is newsworthy in itself

In the House, a bipartisan discharge petition, the parliamentary procedure for going around your own leadership, forced a floor vote on a three-year extension [7]. On January 8, 2026, it passed 230 to 196, with 17 Republicans voting with Democrats [6]. By then the credits had already expired, so the House was technically voting to un-expire them, which is like voting to un-ring a bell, except the bell was millions of people's premiums.

Then the bill went to the Senate, where lawmakers from both parties expected it to fail [7]. A bipartisan Senate group worked on a compromise called the CARE Act, which would bring the bigger credits back for two years with minimum premium payments and income caps [7]. It's been "nearing finalization" since roughly the invention of the phrase "nearing finalization." Meanwhile, insurers filing their 2027 rates projected the expired credits would keep pushing premiums up [3]. Insurers, it turns out, are the only people in this story who planned for the actual future.

## What it cost: the receipts

When the credits went away, the bill came due for real people. Average premium payments after subsidies rose 58 percent for people who signed up for 2026 coverage [2]. Effectuated enrollment, meaning people who actually paid and kept their plans, fell from 21.8 million in February 2025 to 19.2 million in February 2026 [2]. That's about 2.6 million people who looked at the new price, did the math, and decided their health plan was now "hope."

Every state saw enrollment fall except New Mexico [2]. Ohio and Oklahoma dropped just over 32 percent, Arizona 30, South Carolina 29, Indiana 28 [2]. In Mississippi, only 61 percent of people who picked a plan ended up paying for it [2].

New Mexico was the exception because it fully replaced the lost federal credits with its own money [11]. Its enrollment rose 14 percent [2]. So there was a control group, and the control group did fine. Science is so rude sometimes.

And it's not over. For 2027, insurers proposed a median premium increase of 15 percent, across 276 insurers in all 50 states and D.C., the second straight year of double-digit requests [3]. Insurers say the expired credits add about 4 percentage points to 2027 premiums, on top of about 4 points in 2026, because the people who left were likely the healthier ones [3][4]. UnitedHealthcare told New York regulators that policy changes and the subsidy expiration "account for 12.7% of the requested rate change" [4]. KFF's Cynthia Cox called it a "triple whammy" for consumers [4].

Here's one example from KFF's own math. A 40-year-old in Indianapolis making $65,000 paid $316 a month in 2025 [3]. That went to $477 in 2026, and if the 2027 rates are approved, $546 [3]. That's $158 more a month in two years, a 41 percent raise for the insurance company that the customer never asked to give [3].

## The cliff is back, and it's a real cliff

The enhanced credits did one quietly huge thing: they removed the cutoff at 400 percent of the poverty line [7]. Now the regular subsidies mostly stop again at that line, about $62,600 for a single person this year [4]. Earn a dollar under it and you get help. Earn a dollar over it and you're on your own, paying full price. It's the only part of American life where a small raise can make you poorer, other than buying a boat.

The people in the middle feel it most. The Associated Press this weekend told the story of Cindy Banda, a single mother in McAllen, Texas, recovering from breast cancer, who has paid or is paying off more than $25,000 in medical costs, and she has insurance through her job [1]. She's met her deductible this year and will owe about $7,500 again in January [1]. About half of registered voters now call health care costs a major problem for their families, up from a little more than a third four years ago, according to Fox News polling cited by the AP [1]. Her family motto, per the AP: "Keep the house. Keep the cars. And just keep the kids stable" [1]. That's not a health plan. That's a hostage negotiation with three demands.

## "Fraud," and what got built in its name

The case against the credits wasn't only about money. The Congressional Budget Office estimated that making them permanent would add about $350 billion to deficits by 2035 and cover about 3.8 million more people [9]. That is real money, and a fair thing to argue about. Republicans also argued fraud. The Paragon Health Institute, a Republican-aligned think tank, pointed to federal data showing the share of marketplace enrollments with no claims rose from 19 percent in 2021 to 35 percent in 2024, and blamed brokers signing people up without their knowledge [10]. Speaker Mike Johnson called the subsidies "a boondoggle," and Vice President JD Vance cited "waste and fraud" [10].

Some of that is real: news investigations found brokers in some states could enroll people in zero-cost plans without their knowledge [10]. But KFF's Cox pointed out that the data counts enrollments, not people, so someone who switched plans can show up twice, and that "plenty of people don't use health care" [10]. Even the Cato Institute's Michael Cannon said Paragon was "overinterpreting" the numbers [10]. When the libertarians say you're overdoing it on the anti-government case, check your math.

And here's the part that should make everyone mad: the response to "brokers are cheating" mostly landed on customers. HHS's 2027 marketplace rule, finalized in May, tightens income reporting and verification, which Undue Medical Debt says HHS estimates will cost taxpayers about $1.34 billion a year, and HHS estimates it could reduce enrollment by up to 2 million people [11][13]. It permanently ends the special enrollment period for low-income people [11]. It lets catastrophic plans, now with out-of-pocket maximums of $12,000 for an individual, run for up to 10 years [11][13]. A White House spokesperson promised to "hold big insurance companies accountable" [4]. So far, the accountability has mostly arrived as paperwork for the customers.

## Who benefits?

That's the strange part. Insurers lose customers, and the ones who stay pay more [2][3]. Patients pay more or go without [2]. The Treasury saves money, roughly the $350 billion over a decade the CBO priced a permanent extension at, in exchange for about 3.8 million fewer people with coverage [9]. The winners are mostly campaign consultants, who now have an issue to run on from both directions. Democrats get to run against premiums they set up to expire. Republicans get to run against a program while their own Senate candidates sound off about health costs; in Texas, Republican Ken Paxton has proposed a $25,000 tax deduction for out-of-pocket medical expenses, while Democrat James Talarico wants everyone to be able to join Medicare [1].

The health care industry takes in more than $5 trillion a year [1]. The fight over whether to help 20-odd million people buy part of it has been run like a group project where everyone agrees the deadline was yesterday and nobody opened the document.

## What would fix it

This one isn't a mystery, which may be the most infuriating part.

First, Congress can pass something. The House already passed a three-year extension with 230 votes [6]. The Senate's bipartisan CARE Act framework, two years of credits with income caps and minimum premiums, is a compromise both parties' negotiators have actually worked on [7]. Pick one. Vote on it. It's already been written.

Second, stop building health policy that expires in an election year. Temporary credits produced a 2025 cliff, a 2026 premium spike and a 2027 sequel [3][7]. If a benefit is worth having, make it permanent and pay for it. If it isn't, say so. What doesn't work is a coverage policy that runs like a free trial with a surprise auto-renewal.

Third, go after the fraud where it lives. The problem the data points to is brokers enrolling people without their knowledge [10]. Fix it with broker penalties and consent rules, and the 2027 rule does require a uniform consent form for agents and brokers, which is a good start [11]. Making millions of honest people prove their income again is just the new hassle.

Fourth, states can do it themselves. New Mexico replaced the credits and was the only state whose enrollment grew [11][2]. California, Colorado, Connecticut, Maryland, Massachusetts and Washington stepped in for some income groups [11]. The other states are free to copy the homework.

And in the meantime, if you buy your own coverage, open enrollment for 2027 starts November 1 [11]. Shop. Your plan may have changed, been canceled, or gotten more expensive; hundreds of thousands of enrollees have plans ending in 2026 [12]. Look at the whole price, deductible included, not just the monthly number.

Because the bill for this round of Washington brinkmanship already went out. It just didn't go to Washington. It went to Indianapolis, and McAllen, and Ohio, and about 2.6 million mailboxes that stopped getting insurance cards [2][3][1].
targets: Democrats who wrote the expiration date

pt.title: O precipício dos subsídios: Washington deixou o desconto do seu plano de saúde vencer e mandou a conta para você
pt.dek: Os dois partidos viram chegar o fim dos créditos fiscais ampliados do Obamacare. Os prêmios dispararam, 2,6 milhões de pessoas perderam a cobertura, e os preços de 2027 chegam dois dias antes das eleições de meio de mandato.

de.title: Die Zuschuss-Klippe: Washington ließ den Rabatt auf Ihre Krankenversicherung auslaufen und schickte Ihnen die Rechnung
de.dek: Beide Parteien sahen das Ablaufdatum der erweiterten Obamacare-Steuergutschriften seit Jahren kommen. Die Beiträge stiegen, 2,6 Millionen Menschen verloren ihren Schutz, und die Preise für 2027 kommen zwei Tage vor den Zwischenwahlen.
